column4: The ayah names Thamud's she-camel as a visible sign they wronged and says signs are sent only as تَخْوِيفًا; it supplies the exact warning function the section assigns the camel.
The source section's dictionary form مُعَقِّب is spoken here as لَا مُعَقِّبَ لِحُكْمِهِ: God's judgment has no follower who can reverse it, directly unfolding the finality of 91:15.

مُعَقِّبَاتٌ are placed before and behind a person, and the ayah ends by saying that when God wills harm there is no repeller or protector; it joins the bodily behind/heel image to an irreversible consequence.
God is not questioned about what He does while they are questioned, directly stating the asymmetry by which the Lord need not fear the aftermath of His judgment.
The ayah explicitly makes the عَاقِبَة of the nine men's plot their own destruction together with their people, the exact Thamud instance of an act carrying its end behind it.
فَكُلًّا أَخَذْنَا بِذَنبِهِ makes each destroyed people be seized by its own sin, then distinguishes the concrete forms in which that consequence arrived.
The deniers are destroyed بِذُنُوبِهِمْ and Pharaoh's people drowned; this is the same causal wording as 91:14 and makes the punishment the second thing following denial.
God seizes Pharaoh's people and their predecessors بِذُنُوبِهِمْ, then calls Him شَدِيدُ ٱلْعِقَابِ; the ayah itself joins the section's sin and following-punishment roots.
The Pharaoh pattern is repeated as God seizing them بِذُنُوبِهِمْ and being severe in ٱلْعِقَابِ, an explicit lexical meeting of offense and its sequel.
فَأَهْلَكْنَاهُم بِذُنُوبِهِمْ exactly repeats destruction because of sins and then describes another generation raised after them, sharpening the sequence of deed, end, and successor.
Earlier peoples were seized بِذُنُوبِهِمْ and had no protector against God; the causal phrase and failed defense both support the section's unavoidable aftermath.
Salih calls her نَاقَةُ ٱللَّهِ and God's sign, then warns that touching her with harm will bring a near punishment; ownership, trespass, warning, and consequence are all explicit.
After they hamstring the camel, Salih gives them three days and calls the deadline a promise that will not be falsified, exactly staging the delayed but uncancellable end described in the section.
The camel is نَاقَةُ ٱللَّهِ and a sign, allowed to eat on God's earth, while harm to her is tied immediately to painful punishment; the owner's creature and the owner's response stand together.
Thamud hamstring the camel, defy their Lord's command, and demand the threatened result; this gives the precise crime whose consequence the image places at its heel.
The earthquake takes them and leaves them fallen in their home, supplying the concrete outcome of the camel-killing and challenge in 7:77.
The blast seizes the wrongdoers and leaves them fallen in their dwellings, contributing the actual punishment that fulfills the three-day word of 11:65.
Thamud's end is pictured as if they had never flourished in their homes; the ayah completes 11:65 by making the promised sequel erase the offenders' settled life.
Salih identifies the camel and her allotted drink alongside the people's allotted day; with 26:156 it specifies the protected property and measured right they violate.
The command not to touch the camel with harm is coupled to seizure by the punishment of a tremendous day, directly binding trespass to its warned end.
They hamstring her and then become regretful, making remorse the first consequence immediately behind the crime before the punishment of 26:158.
The punishment takes the camel-killers after their regret in 26:157, completing the section's sequence from offense to inescapable recompense.
God says He is sending the camel as a trial and commands watchful patience, making the animal itself the warning-sign before Thamud's choice.
The water is apportioned and every share must be attended, specifying the owner's measured provision that the attack on the camel disrupts in 54:29.
They call their companion, who takes hold and hamstrings the camel; this is the offense whose warned consequence the next two ayat unfold.
God asks how His punishment and warnings were, explicitly interpreting the camel event in 54:27-29 as warning followed by punishment.
A single blast reduces the people to dry crushed material after the hamstringing, a vivid form of the total leveling named in 91:14.
Nine men are identified in the city as corrupters who do not set things right; this supplies the criminal band whose plot reaches its عَاقِبَة in 27:51.
The nine swear to kill Salih and his family at night and then lie to his heir, specifying the guilty act whose terminal result 27:51 tells the reader to inspect.
They devise a plot and God devises one while they do not perceive it, showing the hidden counter-sequence already following their crime before 27:51 announces its end.
Their houses stand empty because they wronged, leaving a visible remainder of the destruction stated in 27:51 and making the crime legible through its aftermath.
Thamud choose blindness over guidance, so a thunderbolt of humiliating punishment seizes them بِمَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ; choice and earned outcome are explicitly joined.
Thamud are told to enjoy themselves only until a stated time, another formulation of the limited interval between the offense and its promised end.
They rebel against their Lord's command, and the thunderbolt takes them while they look on; the verse makes defiance and consequence one continuous scene.
They can neither rise nor obtain help after the thunderbolt, showing that nothing can turn back the judgment once its end arrives.
God destroys Thamud and leaves none, restating the total reach of the Lord's recompense after the camel crime.
Thamud are destroyed by the overwhelming blast, a compressed statement of the people's terminal consequence.

Bad deeds receive an equal recompense, humiliation overtakes their doers, and their faces are as though covered with dark pieces of night; this ayah fuses consequence, غ ش و covering, and the section's night image.
Layers of fire lie above and below them, and بِذَٰلِكَ يُخَوِّفُ ٱللَّهُ عِبَادَهُ says God uses that enclosing end to warn His servants, joining covering punishment to divine fear-making.
Punishment covers them from above and from beneath their feet, and they are told to taste what they did; the surrounding penalty is explicitly their deed's result.
The ayah asks whether they feel safe from a غَاشِيَةٌ مِّنْ عَذَابِ ٱللَّهِ or a sudden Hour, exactly supplying the section's dictionary image of an all-covering divine punishment.
Hell is both bedding below and coverings above, followed by وَكَذَٰلِكَ نَجْزِى ٱلظَّالِمِينَ; enclosure is expressly the wrongdoers' recompense.
The criminals wear pitch and fire تَغْشَىٰ وُجُوهَهُم; with 14:51 this makes covering the bodily form taken by recompense.
God repays every soul what it earned immediately after fire is said to cover the criminals' faces in 14:50, identifying the cover as the act's due sequel.
Whoever earns an evil and is encompassed by his offense becomes a companion of the Fire; the offense itself closes around its doer and carries him to its end.
The evils of what they did strike them and what they mocked surrounds them, turning the deed into the enclosing consequence that follows it.
The evil results of what they earned become manifest and the punishment they mocked surrounds them, a direct formulation of the hidden end emerging from the act.
The evil results of their deeds appear and what they mocked encloses them, repeating the section's movement from crime to an all-around sequel.
The عَاقِبَة of those who did evil is ٱلسُّوٓأَىٰ because they denied God's signs and mocked them; the ayah defines wrongdoing through the bad end carried by denial.
Whatever affliction befalls people is because of what their hands earned, while God pardons much; it states the causal relation by which a painful aftermath follows the act.
Whoever does evil is recompensed for it and finds no protector or helper against God, joining deed, due result, and inability to avert it.
Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, giving bodily force to the section's claim that the deed remains attached until its consequence.
The record makes the guilty fearful, omits neither small nor great, and leaves them finding what they did present; their feared future is their own deed made inescapably present.
The proud gardener's fruit is encompassed by ruin and he turns his hands over what he spent; the act's hidden end becomes visible before 18:44 names the true owner and best outcome.
He has no company to help him against God and cannot defend himself, contributing the no-reversal element between the ruin of 18:42 and God's final authority in 18:44.
At the ruined garden, authority belongs to God alone and He is best in reward and عُقْبًا; ownership and the ultimately good outcome meet in the very aftermath of loss.
وَٱلَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَىٰ repeats the section's night-covering act almost verbatim, and this surah then divides human striving by the ease or hardship to which it leads.
God promises to ease the giving, Godfearing believer of 92:5-6 toward ease, directly expressing the section's good, non-heavy end of purification.
God eases the miserly denier of 92:8-9 toward hardship, giving the negative counterpart: a chosen act carries a hard end behind it.
قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ repeats both purification and success from 91:9, and 87:16-17 immediately disclose why that purified course has the better end.
Whoever purifies himself does so only for his own good, and the destination is to God; purification is explicitly defined by whom its outcome returns to and where it ends.
Patient worshippers who answer evil with good are promised عُقْبَى ٱلدَّارِ, making the end attached to purified conduct the reverse of Thamud's end.
The angels greet the patient with peace and call their destination نِعْمَ عُقْبَى ٱلدَّارِ, naming the good sequel of the conduct listed in 13:22.
The final home is for those who seek neither self-exaltation nor corruption, and وَٱلْعَاقِبَةُ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ makes their good end the specific reverse of a corrupting people's ruin.
One who submits to God while doing good grasps the firmest handhold, and to God belongs عَاقِبَةُ ٱلْأُمُورِ; sound action and the final end of affairs are joined.
God's ownership of the heavens and earth is stated immediately before His freedom to punish or forgive, directly supporting the section's movement from owner to recompense.
What is in heaven and earth belongs to God; hidden and open contents are brought to account, after which He forgives or punishes, making ownership the frame of judgment.
Heaven and earth belong to God so that He may recompense evildoers for what they did and reward good-doers with the best, explicitly deriving the two outcomes from His ownership.
On the day all are exposed, God asks whose sovereignty is His and answers that it belongs to the One, the Subduer; 40:17 then makes this ownership the setting of final recompense.
Every soul is repaid for what it earned, with no injustice and swift account, supplying the just consequence under the sole sovereignty declared in 40:16.
People are returned to God, their true master; judgment belongs to Him and He is swift in account, joining ownership, return, and the final ruling after which nothing remains.
No soul owns anything for another on the Day, and the command belongs wholly to God, isolating the Owner whose judgment no one can answer or reverse.
The punishment of the Lord is declared certain to occur, the promised finality whose second half is supplied by 52:8.
مَا لَهُۥ مِن دَافِعٍ says the certain punishment of 52:7 has no repeller, matching the section's claim that no one can turn back the end.
A questioner asks for the punishment that is bound to fall, staging a demanded consequence like Thamud's challenge before 70:2 states its unavoidability.
The punishment for the disbelievers has no averter, directly matching the irrevocable outcome attached to denial.
People are commanded to answer their Lord before a day comes from God that cannot be repelled, turning finality into the same preventive warning the section describes.
God never fails His promise to His messengers and is mighty in retribution, directly supporting the unfalsifiable promise that followed Thamud's crime.
وَٱللَّهُ مِن وَرَآئِهِم مُّحِيطٌ places God behind the persistent deniers and encompassing them, a striking nonlexical meeting of the section's rear/heel and all-covering judgment images.
A good deed receives better, while those who bring an evil are repaid only for what they did; the ayah states both the easy good end and the bounded bad sequel.
An evil deed receives only its like, while righteous believers enter the Garden without measure; it sets the two opposed outcomes beside their generating acts.
The punishment is identified as what their hands sent ahead, and God denies injustice to His servants; the result is the offender's own act arriving before him.
The same formula says the punishment is what their hands sent ahead and that God does not wrong His servants, defining the consequence as earned rather than arbitrary.

Unlike the night-covered faces of evildoers in 10:27, the good-doers' faces are covered by neither darkness nor humiliation; this is the section's digestible good end pictured as the absence of a punitive cover.
People prefer the nearer worldly life immediately after 87:14 praises purification, identifying the short preference that can obscure the purified person's true outcome.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting than the nearer life of 87:16, clarifying why purification in 87:14 has the end that remains rather than the one that passes.

Moses says the Egyptians hold a ذَنبٌ against him and therefore he fears they will kill him; a human agent expects a harmful sequel to an offense, precisely reversing God's lack of fear after judgment.
Moses says he killed one of them and fears they will kill him, restaging fear as expectation that an adverse consequence will follow one's prior act.
Those who feel secure from God's plan are called losers; their false absence of fear is the human opposite of the Lord's rightful lack of fear about His decree.
The murdered girl is asked for what ذَنبٍ she was killed; the unanswered question marks the boundary that a just punishment follows an actual offense, not an innocent victim.

Human retaliation, عَاقِبُوا, is limited to the like of what was suffered and patience is called better; the penalty-after-offense root is retained while human recompense is placed under a strict boundary.
One who retaliates only in the measure suffered and is then attacked is promised God's help; the ayah bounds human punishment even while using the section's following-recompense root.

After recalling earlier generations destroyed by God, the ayah says criminals are not asked about their ذُنُوبِهِمْ; in context this marks judgment that needs no fact-finding, a boundary beside 21:23's broader accountability claim.

ذَنُوبًا here means an allotted share rather than sins: wrongdoers have a share like their predecessors', so the source section's root sounds within a promised portion of the very consequence it describes.
ٱلْغَاشِيَةِ names the overwhelming event whose following verses describe humbled faces and fire, extending the section's غ ش و branch from night's cover to eschatological punishment.
After the overturned cities are cast down in 53:53, فَغَشَّىٰهَا مَا غَشَّىٰ makes an unnamed covering complete their destruction, another punitive use of the section's covering root.
The manifest smoke of 44:10 يَغْشَى ٱلنَّاسَ and is identified as a painful punishment, giving the covering-punishment relation a visible collective form.
God records both what people sent ahead and their آثار, the tracks they leave behind; this offers a concrete trail-image for acts persisting into their later reckoning.
Every soul is commanded to inspect what it has sent ahead for tomorrow, recasting the section's consequence-behind-the-act as a deed already dispatched toward its doer.
A person will be told what he sent ahead and left behind, placing the complete account on both temporal sides of the body-like image developed in the section.
Each soul will know what it sent ahead and left behind, a parallel formulation of deeds retaining a rearward remainder that appears at the final accounting.
If the addressees turn away from God's judgment, He intends to strike them for some of their ذُنُوبِهِمْ; the offense is again named as the cause of the blow that follows.
Heaven and earth belong to God, who forgives or punishes whom He wills; this repeated owner-to-judgment formula supports the section's reading of Rabb as proprietor.
God's sovereignty over heaven and earth is again followed immediately by forgiveness or punishment according to His will, reinforcing ownership as the setting of recompense.
Moses tells his people that the earth belongs to God and that ٱلْعَاقِبَةُ belongs to the Godfearing; ownership and the good end meet, though outside the purification wording itself.
The Prophet is told to be patient because ٱلْعَاقِبَةَ is for the Godfearing, a direct positive counterpart to Thamud's disastrous outcome.
After the command to persist in prayer, وَٱلْعَاقِبَةُ لِلتَّقْوَىٰ states that the enduring end belongs to reverence, matching the section's favorable sequel of purified conduct.
No one can change the Lord's words and no refuge exists besides Him, supporting the section's claim that the final divine word admits neither revision nor escape.
The Lord's word is completed in truth and justice and no one can alter His words, giving the promised outcome its truth and irreversibility.
If God touches someone with harm none can remove it, and if He intends good none can repel His bounty; the ayah states the no-reversal principle on both sides of outcome.
No protector can save from God's command on the flood day except one receiving mercy, a concrete disaster-scene boundary on any attempt to avert divine judgment.
Barriers are set before and behind the deniers and God covers them so they cannot see; this ayah tightly joins the section's bodily rearward image to the غ ش و covering branch.
The condemned person receives his record from behind his back, giving literal bodily placement to the deed-account whose painful end follows in 84:11-12.
The recipient of the record behind his back calls for destruction, contributing the immediate recognition of the bad end attached to that rearward record.
He enters a blazing fire after receiving the record behind his back, completing the bodily sequence from recorded deeds to their consequence.
Moses offers Pharaoh the possibility that he might purify himself; 79:21-25 then show denial taking him to the opposite end, so purification and outcome meet within one scene.
Pharaoh denies and disobeys after the offer of purification in 79:18, specifying the guilty turn whose result arrives in 79:25.
Pharaoh proclaims himself the highest lord, making false ownership and lordship the offense immediately before the true God seizes him.
God seizes Pharaoh with the exemplary punishment of the latter and the former after his refusal to purify and claim to lordship, directly staging deed followed by recompense.
After Thamud's destruction, Salih says he delivered his Lord's message and advised them but they did not love advisers; this completes the camel episode's warning stance.
The completed camel-and-punishment story is declared a sign, and God is named the mighty, merciful Lord; this interprets the event itself as warning under its owner.
After 13:41 denies any reverser of God's judgment, this ayah says all planning belongs to God and disbelievers will learn who has عُقْبَى ٱلدَّارِ; it adds the final outcome of rival plots.
Each person's enduring fate is fastened to his neck and will be brought out as a record, a bodily attachment that makes the later consequence inseparable from the doer.
God creates heaven and earth in truth so that every soul may be repaid for what it earned without injustice, joining the Owner-Creator directly to just consequence.
Whoever does good does it for himself and whoever does evil does it against himself, while the Lord is not unjust; the act already bears the direction of its end.
Each soul earns only against itself, no bearer carries another's burden, and all return to their Lord; this fixes each consequence to its own offender and final Owner.
Good is done for oneself and evil against oneself, then the final promise arrives; the ayah explicitly lets the chosen act carry its later promised end.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, making even the smallest sound act persist to its favorable outcome.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, a minimal and exact statement that an offense remains until it meets its doer.
A person has only what he strove for, grounding the consequence completed in 53:40-41 in the person's own act.
Human striving will be seen, making the once-hidden deed visible before its full repayment in 53:41.
The striving shown in 53:40 is repaid with the fullest recompense, completing the sequence from act to terminal return.
The inhabitants of the Blaze confess their ذَنب, and exclusion is pronounced on them; confession and the sin's terminal punishment stand in the same ayah.
What people were earning forms a rust-like covering over their hearts, so their own repeated acts become the cover that precedes the fire of 83:16.
They enter Hell after their earnings have coated their hearts in 83:14, turning that inward covering into its final punitive result.
The merciful Lord could seize people immediately for what they earned but gives them an appointed time from which they find no escape, closely paralleling Thamud's fixed delay.
If God seized people for wrongdoing no creature would remain, yet He delays them to a term that can be neither postponed nor advanced once it comes.
If God took people for what they earned no creature would remain, but He defers them to an appointed term and then fully sees His servants; delay does not cancel consequence.
The disbelievers ask when the promise will arrive, reproducing the challenger's stance before the fixed answer in 34:30.
The challengers are told they have an appointed day that they can delay or advance by no hour, sharpening the three-day promise's exact finality.
What the addressees are promised is declared true, supporting the section's insistence that the post-crime promise cannot be falsified.
Judgment is declared certain to occur immediately after the promise is called true in 51:5, identifying the promise's unavoidable content.
What people are promised is certain to occur, a compact parallel to the unfalsifiable word given after the camel's killing.
God's promise is true whether the Prophet is shown some threatened punishment or dies before it, since all return to God; non-observation does not undo the result.
The deniers ask to hasten God's punishment, a stance matching Thamud's demand that the warned sequel be brought.
The ayah asks the reader to consider even years of temporary enjoyment, setting up the limited interval before the promise in 26:206.
After the imagined long respite, the promised result comes to them; the lapse between crime and consequence changes neither its truth nor arrival.
Their former enjoyment does not benefit them once the promise comes, showing that what preceded the final judgment cannot stand after it.
The townspeople feel secure from punishment coming by night while they sleep, exposing false human fearlessness before an unexpected consequence.
The townspeople likewise feel secure from punishment arriving by day during play, completing the warning that no ordinary setting makes the threatened end avoidable.
Those who plot evil are asked whether they feel secure from being swallowed by the earth or struck unexpectedly, tying criminal plotting to the danger they fail to fear.
God may seize the plotters amid their movements and they cannot frustrate Him, making the warned consequence impossible to outrun.
Those on earth are asked whether they feel secure from being made to sink into the shaking ground, another warning against the offender's misplaced lack of fear.
They are asked whether they feel secure from a stone-bearing storm and are told they will know how God's warning is, joining threatened sign and fear-making.
Earlier peoples denied, and the ayah asks how God's rejection of them was; it supplies the historical consequence behind the warning in 67:16-17.
People are commanded to set themselves toward the right religion before a day comes from God that cannot be repelled, making finality itself a preventive warning.
Sovereignty over everything is in God's hand; He protects while none can protect against Him, directly uniting ownership with unanswerable judgment.
If the Merciful intends harm, other gods' intercession cannot help and they cannot rescue, stating the no-reversal consequence against imagined rival owners.
The idolaters are asked whether their gods could remove harm intended by God or withhold His mercy, testing both kinds of outcome against His sole authority.
What people possess comes to an end while what is with God remains, and the patient are repaid by their best deeds; it makes permanence the measure of the favorable sequel.
Everything perishes except God, judgment belongs to Him, and all are returned to Him; nothing follows or outlasts the Owner's final ruling.
They deny what they have not comprehended before its fulfillment reaches them, then the reader is told to inspect the عَاقِبَة of the wrongdoers; premature denial carries a later disclosed end.
They reject the signs unjustly despite inward certainty, and the reader is told to see the عَاقِبَة of the corrupters; culpable denial is interpreted by its ending.
Messengers brought clear proofs, people disbelieved, and God seized them as strong and severe in punishment; this supplies the explanatory continuation of the sin-seizure in 40:21.
Messengers are mocked, the disbelievers receive respite, and then God seizes them; the ayah asks how His punishment was, precisely staging delay followed by consequence.
Moses is denied, the deniers receive respite, and then God seizes them; the sequence reinforces that postponement never falsifies the threatened end.
When the command arrives, Salih and the believers are saved by mercy while the camel-killers proceed to disgrace, showing the Lord's judgment distinguishing innocent from guilty.
God saves those who believed and were mindful immediately after the plotters' ruined houses in 27:52, providing the opposite outcome under the same Owner.
Believers who were Godfearing are saved after Thamud is seized for what it earned in 41:17, separating the purified course from the guilty people's end.
A believer who does right fears neither injustice nor diminution, showing the human freedom from fear granted by a sound deed's end rather than the sovereign fearlessness of the Judge.
Those who believe in their Lord fear neither loss nor oppressive burden, a good-outcome counterpart to the offender who rightly expects a harmful sequel.
After the killing, Moses leaves the city fearful and watchful, embodying a human actor's expectation that an adverse result may follow his earlier deed.
Thamud are named with Pharaoh immediately before 85:19-20 describe deniers whom God encompasses from behind; this ayah supplies the specific people for that rearward scene.
The named peoples' ongoing denial is stated just before God encompasses them from behind in 85:20, contributing the offense to which that enclosing position answers.
The audience is told to travel and inspect the عَاقِبَة of the deniers, treating an act of rejection as something understood through its historical end.
Travel through the earth and inspect the عَاقِبَة of the deniers repeats the section's method of reading guilt by the terminal evidence it leaves.
After the punitive rain on Lot's people, the reader is told to inspect the عَاقِبَة of the criminals, explicitly joining crime-language to the end of the scene.
Shuayb's people are told to inspect the عَاقِبَة of corrupters after being warned against blocking and distorting God's way, making the social offense legible in its end.
After Pharaoh's people wrongfully reject the signs, the reader is told to inspect the عَاقِبَة of corrupters, another sign-denial ending in judgment.
Every nation receives a messenger commanding worship and avoidance of false gods, and the reader is told to inspect the عَاقِبَة of the deniers; warning precedes the visible end.
Pharaoh and his hosts are seized and cast into the sea, then the reader is told to see the عَاقِبَة of wrongdoers; the bodily punishment defines the tyranny's end.
People are told to inspect how the عَاقِبَة of stronger earlier civilizations followed their self-wronging despite messengers' proofs.
Travel is commanded to see the عَاقِبَة of former peoples, most of whom associated partners with God; the lasting trace discloses the belief's consequence.
The reader is told to inspect the عَاقِبَة of stronger predecessors and is reminded that nothing can escape God, joining historical ends to irresistible power.
Earlier peoples were stronger and left more traces, yet their acquisitions did not avail; the instruction to inspect their عَاقِبَة makes achievement yield to final consequence.
The reader is told to inspect the عَاقِبَة of former peoples and then that the final home is better for the Godfearing, placing bad historical ends beside the favorable enduring one.
Those established in the land uphold worship and right conduct, and to God belongs عَاقِبَةُ ٱلْأُمُورِ; responsible action is placed before the Owner's final outcome.
A غِشَاوَةٌ lies over the deniers' sight and a great punishment awaits them, a different use of the section's covering root that makes prior blindness lead toward punishment.
One who takes desire as god is knowingly left astray with a covering over sight; the visual cover is a present consequence of chosen misrule under God's judgment.
The punishment of the day of the overshadowing cloud seizes Shuayb's deniers, an indirect collective parallel to punishment arriving in a covering form.
The kindled fire is closed over the offenders, another concrete form of punishment enclosing those whose preceding acts brought it.
A manifest smoke is watched for in the sky, providing the visible substance that covers the people and is named painful punishment in 44:11.
God may seize the plotters through gradual diminution, a secondary use of the fear root's form that adds slow reduction to the sudden punishments of 16:45-46.
Thamud are among peoples whose messengers brought proofs; God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves, placing responsibility for their end on their own act.
Thamud are named among the peoples who denied messengers before the present deniers, supplying a specific precedent for the respite-and-seizure pattern completed in 22:44.
Thamud and the other named peoples deny their messengers, so God's threat becomes due; denial is followed by a promised consequence in compressed form.
Each of the listed peoples denies the messengers and thereby makes God's punishment due, another direct formulation of warning rejected and consequence incurred.
